messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the pediatric emergency with confusion and disorientation. She was diagnosed with bacterial meningitis based on clinical examination and CSF analysis and was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin. A CT scan was performed, and pneumocephalus was observed in the right frontal region. The patient was treated for signs of chronic sinusitis and pansinusitis. She showed initial symptomatic improvements to antibiotics but suffered a deterioration of her GCS to 7/15, with a high-grade fever.

Subdural empyema was diagnosed through a repeat CT scan, requiring immediate neurosurgical intervention. The surgical drainage was performed, and on the second day, the patient's GCS improved to 15/15, and her fever had subsided. The patient was discharged with a prescription for oral antibiotics, nasal saline spray, and nasal decongestants.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
The patient received intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin to treat bacterial meningitis. Subdural empyema was treated through immediate neurosurgical intervention, which involved surgical drainage. The patient was prescribed oral antibiotics, nasal saline spray, and nasal decongestants upon discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient was seen at two-week and four-week follow-ups and experienced significant improvements in symptoms.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for this admission is bacterial meningitis, diagnosed on presentation from clinical examination and CSF analysis and treated with IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin. The subdural empyema appeared later in the stay as a complication, and the sinusitis is the underlying source, so neither is the principal diagnosis. Bacterial meningitis falls in chapter G, category G00.

CODE: G00
